ABSTRACT

We present a machine unlearning approach that is both retraining- and label-free.
Most existing machine unlearning approaches require a model to be fine-tuned
to remove information while preserving performance. This is computationally
expensive and necessitates the storage of the whole dataset for the lifetime of
the model. Retraining-free approaches often utilise Fisher information, which
is derived from the loss and requires labelled data which may not be available.
Thus, we present an extension to the Selective Synaptic Dampening algorithm,
substituting the diagonal of the Fisher information matrix for the gradient of the
l2 norm of the model output to approximate sensitivity. We evaluate our method
in a range of experiments using ResNet18 and Vision Transformer. Results show
our label-free method is competitive with existing state-of-the-art approaches.

1 I NTRODUCTION & RELATED WORK

With increasing regulations around machine learning, the ability for a trained model to forget private
or harmful information is essential. This task is typically formulated by splitting some training
dataset D into a subset of data that needs to be forgotten Df , and the retained data Dr = D \ Df .
The objective is to forget Df from the model, while simultaneously preserving model performance
on Dr (Cao & Yang, 2015). To solve this problem, several methods have been proposed that disrupt
the model’s functional mapping for samples in Df (e.g. by learning random labels), while also
training for a small number of epochs over Dr to repair or protect performance (Chundawat et al.,
2023a;b; Graves et al., 2021; Tarun et al., 2023; Kurmanji et al., 2023). This is computationally
expensive and requires the storage of the full dataset permanently. In contrast, recent methods such
as FisherForgetting from Golatkar et al. (2020) or Selective Synaptic Dampening (SSD) from Foster
et al. (2023) have explored retraining-free approaches, with the latter achieving state-of-the-art
performance. These often involve estimating the importance of parameters for the forget set,
allowing them to be disrupted through noise or dampening, but without destroying performance
on the retain set. Parameter importance estimation is typically achieved via the diagonal of the
Fisher information matrix (FIM), which in practice is calculated as the square of the first-order
gradients of the loss. This requires access to a ground truth label, which may not always be
available. Therefore, we propose a novel extension of SSD that does not require access to the loss
or ground truth labels, which we refer to as Loss-Free Selective Synaptic Dampening (LFSSD).
LFSSD replaces the Fisher-based importance estimation with an approximation of the sensitivity of
the model to perturbations of each parameter, which may be interpreted as parameter importance.
Such importance estimation has been shown to be effective in continual learning (Aljundi et al.,
2018), yet it has not been applied in unlearning. Here, we show this new approach to dampening
important parameters is equally effective as Fisher information, without relying on labelled data.
To the best of our knowledge, LFSSD is the first retraining-free unlearning method to require only
the unlabelled forget samples at forgetting time.

We build upon the approach presented in SSD (Foster et al., 2023). Given the parameter importance
over both D and Df , we can select parameters that are disproportionately important for the forget
set, and reduce their magnitude to induce forgetting in the model:

Here, α and λ are hyper-parameters, and []Df,i and []Di are the ith element of the diagonal of
the FIM, calculated over Df and D, respectively. Fisher information is calculated over D not Dr,
meaning this is only calculated once, and then the train-set may be discarded after. We replace
the Fisher information with the sensitivity estimation from Aljundi et al. (2018), which we now
introduce. Given some neural network output, f (x; θ), and some small perturbation δ = {δi} in the

of the gradient. For multi-dimensional outputs, this gradient must be calculated over every dimen-

Which we can calculate over D and Df and substitute into equation 1 in place of [] and []f . Results
can be seen in Table 1, with further results available in the appendix. The objective is to maximise
the Dr accuracy while having a low membership inference attack score (MIA) similar to the retrain
column (Shokri et al., 2017). Similarity to the retrained model is necessary, as ”over-forgetting” can
lead to the Streisand effect (e.g., labelling a cat as a boat is an obvious modification) (Chundawat
et al., 2023a). The results show that LFSSD produces scores similar to that of a model trained
on only Dr, and is competitive with state-of-the-art methods such as SSD, while being the first
method to require no labelled data and no retraining. A shared limitation with SSD is the reliance
on choosing α and λ values that balance forgetting and model performance.

3 C ONCLUSION

Developing lightweight yet effective machine unlearning approaches is a significant open problem.
In this work, we presented a novel extension of existing literature that is the first retraining free
machine unlearning method to require only the unlabelled input samples for the forget set. By not
requiring the long-term storage of the retain dataset, a labelled forget set, or the loss over the forget
set, LFSSD is lightweight, robust and more practically useful than its predecessors.

Benchmarks. We evaluate LFSSD in the same manner as Chundawat et al. (2023a); Foster et al.
(2023), comparing against a baseline model without any unlearning, a model retrained from scratch
on only Dr, a model finetuned for 2 epochs on Dr, and several existing state-of-the-art methods
(Chundawat et al., 2023a; Graves et al., 2021; Foster et al., 2023) (teacher, amnesiac, SSD). Three
key tasks are evaluated using ResNet18 (RN) and Vision Transformer (ViT): full class, subclass,
and random forgetting. Fullclass entails forgetting an entire class from the dataset (e.g. rocket from
Cifar100), subclass involves forgetting a related subclass from the dataset (e.g. all rockets from class
Vehicle2 in Cifar20), and random forgetting selects a random subset of samples across all classes.
Datasets used include the Cifar suite (Krizhevsky & Hinton, 2010), and the PINS face recognition
dataset (Burak, 2020). Runs are repeated 10 times for each method, with the mean and standard
deviation shown in the tables. Dr and Df in the tables denote the accuracy on the respective subset
of data in percent. Since SSD (and therefore LFSSD) is deterministic, there is no standard deviation

Resources. A single backward pass over the full dataset D is O(bf ull· p) where bf ullis the number
of batches in the dataset and p is the number of parameters in the model. Similarly, the complexity
for the forget and retain set is O(bf orget· p) and O(bretain · p), respectively. Note that bretain ≈
bf ull>> bf orget. SSD requires only one computation of the gradients for D (can be saved and
reused), then for every forget request it requires one computation forDf to then apply the dampening
in O(bf orget· p).

LFSSD has the same complexity as SSD with the difference being that LFSSD calculates the norm
of the output instead of the loss. In practice, this is similar in compute time.

Other methods are retraining-based and depend on the number of epochs N, generally on the order
of O(N · bretain · p), which is much larger.

Sensitivity analysis. The values for alpha and lambda for SSD are taken from Foster et al. (2023)
where the authors used Optuna to search for ideal parameters. For LFSSD we performed a simplified
hyperparameter search keeping lambda fixed at 1 and alpha values [1, 50]. We pick one value per
unlearning task (e.g. full class, sub-class, random) to show robustness across classes and do not
use the best alpha per individual class/subclass (e.g., taking alpha 25 for rocket, alpha 5 for another
class, etc.). A sensitivity analysis in Table 2 on CIFAR100 rocket class unlearning shows that there
is a significant drop off in performance when picking an alpha that is too aggressive or conservative
but the method has a wide plateau in which it performs well.

Unlearning scenarios without labels. For cases where labels are hard to get we expect two main
scenarios: First, having a catalogue of undesired/copyrighted data (e.g., images) that we want to
unlearn from the model just to be on the safe side legally even if it might not be in the model. In this
case, we do not have the labels. Second, models that were trained with semi-supervised learning
could benefit from our method when we do not want to rely on the accuracy of pseudo labels.

Developing lightweight yet effective machine unlearning approaches is a significant open problem.
In this work, we presented a novel extension of existing literature that is the first retraining free

ABSTRACT

We present a machine unlearning approach that is both retraining- and label-free.
Most existing machine unlearning approaches require a model to be fine-tuned
to remove information while preserving performance. This is computationally
expensive and necessitates the storage of the whole dataset for the lifetime of
the model. Retraining-free approaches often utilise Fisher information, which
is derived from the loss and requires labelled data which may not be available.
Thus, we present an extension to the Selective Synaptic Dampening algorithm,
substituting the diagonal of the Fisher information matrix for the gradient of the
l2 norm of the model output to approximate sensitivity. We evaluate our method
in a range of experiments using ResNet18 and Vision Transformer. Results show
our label-free method is competitive with existing state-of-the-art approaches.
excerpts.heading: ABSTRACT

excerpts.text:
1 I NTRODUCTION & RELATED WORK

With increasing regulations around machine learning, the ability for a trained model to forget private
or harmful information is essential. This task is typically formulated by splitting some training
dataset D into a subset of data that needs to be forgotten Df , and the retained data Dr = D \ Df .
The objective is to forget Df from the model, while simultaneously preserving model performance
on Dr (Cao & Yang, 2015). To solve this problem, several methods have been proposed that disrupt
the model’s functional mapping for samples in Df (e.g. by learning random labels), while also
training for a small number of epochs over Dr to repair or protect performance (Chundawat et al.,
2023a;b; Graves et al., 2021; Tarun et al., 2023; Kurmanji et al., 2023). This is computationally
expensive and requires the storage of the full dataset permanently. In contrast, recent methods such
as FisherForgetting from Golatkar et al. (2020) or Selective Synaptic Dampening (SSD) from Foster
et al. (2023) have explored retraining-free approaches, with the latter achieving state-of-the-art
performance. These often involve estimating the importance of parameters for the forget set,
allowing them to be disrupted through noise or dampening, but without destroying performance
on the retain set. Parameter importance estimation is typically achieved via the diagonal of the
Fisher information matrix (FIM), which in practice is calculated as the square of the first-order
gradients of the loss. This requires access to a ground truth label, which may not always be
available. Therefore, we propose a novel extension of SSD that does not require access to the loss
or ground truth labels, which we refer to as Loss-Free Selective Synaptic Dampening (LFSSD).
LFSSD replaces the Fisher-based importance estimation with an approximation of the sensitivity of
the model to perturbations of each parameter, which may be interpreted as parameter importance.
Such importance estimation has been shown to be effective in continual learning (Aljundi et al.,
2018), yet it has not been applied in unlearning. Here, we show this new approach to dampening
important parameters is equally effective as Fisher information, without relying on labelled data.
To the best of our knowledge, LFSSD is the first retraining-free unlearning method to require only
the unlabelled forget samples at forgetting time.

Benchmarks. We evaluate LFSSD in the same manner as Chundawat et al. (2023a); Foster et al.
(2023), comparing against a baseline model without any unlearning, a model retrained from scratch
on only Dr, a model finetuned for 2 epochs on Dr, and several existing state-of-the-art methods
(Chundawat et al., 2023a; Graves et al., 2021; Foster et al., 2023) (teacher, amnesiac, SSD). Three
key tasks are evaluated using ResNet18 (RN) and Vision Transformer (ViT): full class, subclass,
and random forgetting. Fullclass entails forgetting an entire class from the dataset (e.g. rocket from
Cifar100), subclass involves forgetting a related subclass from the dataset (e.g. all rockets from class
Vehicle2 in Cifar20), and random forgetting selects a random subset of samples across all classes.
Datasets used include the Cifar suite (Krizhevsky & Hinton, 2010), and the PINS face recognition
dataset (Burak, 2020). Runs are repeated 10 times for each method, with the mean and standard
deviation shown in the tables. Dr and Df in the tables denote the accuracy on the respective subset

Resources. A single backward pass over the full dataset D is O(bf ull· p) where bf ullis the number
of batches in the dataset and p is the number of parameters in the model. Similarly, the complexity
for the forget and retain set is O(bf orget· p) and O(bretain · p), respectively. Note that bretain ≈
bf ull>> bf orget. SSD requires only one computation of the gradients for D (can be saved and
reused), then for every forget request it requires one computation forDf to then apply the dampening
in O(bf orget· p).

LFSSD has the same complexity as SSD with the difference being that LFSSD calculates the norm
of the output instead of the loss. In practice, this is similar in compute time.

Other methods are retraining-based and depend on the number of epochs N, generally on the order
of O(N · bretain · p), which is much larger.

Sensitivity analysis. The values for alpha and lambda for SSD are taken from Foster et al. (2023)
where the authors used Optuna to search for ideal parameters. For LFSSD we performed a simplified
hyperparameter search keeping lambda fixed at 1 and alpha values [1, 50]. We pick one value per
unlearning task (e.g. full class, sub-class, random) to show robustness across classes and do not
use the best alpha per individual class/subclass (e.g., taking alpha 25 for rocket, alpha 5 for another
class, etc.). A sensitivity analysis in Table 2 on CIFAR100 rocket class unlearning shows that there
is a significant drop off in performance when picking an alpha that is too aggressive or conservative
but the method has a wide plateau in which it performs well.

Unlearning scenarios without labels. For cases where labels are hard to get we expect two main
scenarios: First, having a catalogue of undesired/copyrighted data (e.g., images) that we want to
unlearn from the model just to be on the safe side legally even if it might not be in the model. In this
case, we do not have the labels. Second, models that were trained with semi-supervised learning
could benefit from our method when we do not want to rely on the accuracy of pseudo labels.

for the forget and retain set is O(bf orget· p) and O(bretain · p), respectively. Note that bretain ≈
bf ull>> bf orget. SSD requires only one computation of the gradients for D (can be saved and
reused), then for every forget request it requires one computation forDf to then apply the dampening
in O(bf orget· p).

LFSSD has the same complexity as SSD with the difference being that LFSSD calculates the norm
of the output instead of the loss. In practice, this is similar in compute time.

Other methods are retraining-based and depend on the number of epochs N, generally on the order
of O(N · bretain · p), which is much larger.

Sensitivity analysis. The values for alpha and lambda for SSD are taken from Foster et al. (2023)
where the authors used Optuna to search for ideal parameters. For LFSSD we performed a simplified
hyperparameter search keeping lambda fixed at 1 and alpha values [1, 50]. We pick one value per
unlearning task (e.g. full class, sub-class, random) to show robustness across classes and do not
use the best alpha per individual class/subclass (e.g., taking alpha 25 for rocket, alpha 5 for another
class, etc.). A sensitivity analysis in Table 2 on CIFAR100 rocket class unlearning shows that there
is a significant drop off in performance when picking an alpha that is too aggressive or conservative
but the method has a wide plateau in which it performs well.

Unlearning scenarios without labels. For cases where labels are hard to get we expect two main
scenarios: First, having a catalogue of undesired/copyrighted data (e.g., images) that we want to
unlearn from the model just to be on the safe side legally even if it might not be in the model. In this
case, we do not have the labels. Second, models that were trained with semi-supervised learning
could benefit from our method when we do not want to rely on the accuracy of pseudo labels.

LOSS -FREE MACHINE UNLEARNING

Jack Foster∗1,2, Stefan Schoepf ∗1,2 & Alexandra Brintrup 1,2
1Department of Engineering, University of Cambridge
2The Alan Turing Institute
*Indicates equal contribution
{jwf40,ss2823,ab702}@cam.ac.uk
excerpts.heading: Accepted as a Tiny Paper at ICLR 2024 (Preprint)

excerpts.text:
ABSTRACT

We present a machine unlearning approach that is both retraining- and label-free.
Most existing machine unlearning approaches require a model to be fine-tuned
to remove information while preserving performance. This is computationally
expensive and necessitates the storage of the whole dataset for the lifetime of
the model. Retraining-free approaches often utilise Fisher information, which
is derived from the loss and requires labelled data which may not be available.
Thus, we present an extension to the Selective Synaptic Dampening algorithm,
substituting the diagonal of the Fisher information matrix for the gradient of the
l2 norm of the model output to approximate sensitivity. We evaluate our method
in a range of experiments using ResNet18 and Vision Transformer. Results show
our label-free method is competitive with existing state-of-the-art approaches.
excerpts.heading: ABSTRACT

excerpts.text:
1 I NTRODUCTION & RELATED WORK

With increasing regulations around machine learning, the ability for a trained model to forget private
or harmful information is essential. This task is typically formulated by splitting some training
dataset D into a subset of data that needs to be forgotten Df , and the retained data Dr = D \ Df .
The objective is to forget Df from the model, while simultaneously preserving model performance
on Dr (Cao & Yang, 2015). To solve this problem, several methods have been proposed that disrupt
the model’s functional mapping for samples in Df (e.g. by learning random labels), while also
training for a small number of epochs over Dr to repair or protect performance (Chundawat et al.,
2023a;b; Graves et al., 2021; Tarun et al., 2023; Kurmanji et al., 2023). This is computationally
expensive and requires the storage of the full dataset permanently. In contrast, recent methods such
as FisherForgetting from Golatkar et al. (2020) or Selective Synaptic Dampening (SSD) from Foster
et al. (2023) have explored retraining-free approaches, with the latter achieving state-of-the-art
performance. These often involve estimating the importance of parameters for the forget set,
allowing them to be disrupted through noise or dampening, but without destroying performance
on the retain set. Parameter importance estimation is typically achieved via the diagonal of the
Fisher information matrix (FIM), which in practice is calculated as the square of the first-order
gradients of the loss. This requires access to a ground truth label, which may not always be
available. Therefore, we propose a novel extension of SSD that does not require access to the loss
or ground truth labels, which we refer to as Loss-Free Selective Synaptic Dampening (LFSSD).
LFSSD replaces the Fisher-based importance estimation with an approximation of the sensitivity of
the model to perturbations of each parameter, which may be interpreted as parameter importance.
Such importance estimation has been shown to be effective in continual learning (Aljundi et al.,
2018), yet it has not been applied in unlearning. Here, we show this new approach to dampening
important parameters is equally effective as Fisher information, without relying on labelled data.
To the best of our knowledge, LFSSD is the first retraining-free unlearning method to require only
the unlabelled forget samples at forgetting time.

1

Which we can calculate over D and Df and substitute into equation 1 in place of [] and []f . Results
can be seen in Table 1, with further results available in the appendix. The objective is to maximise
the Dr accuracy while having a low membership inference attack score (MIA) similar to the retrain
column (Shokri et al., 2017). Similarity to the retrained model is necessary, as ”over-forgetting” can
lead to the Streisand effect (e.g., labelling a cat as a boat is an obvious modification) (Chundawat
et al., 2023a). The results show that LFSSD produces scores similar to that of a model trained
on only Dr, and is competitive with state-of-the-art methods such as SSD, while being the first
method to require no labelled data and no retraining. A shared limitation with SSD is the reliance
on choosing α and λ values that balance forgetting and model performance.

excerpts.text:
3 C ONCLUSION

Developing lightweight yet effective machine unlearning approaches is a significant open problem.
In this work, we presented a novel extension of existing literature that is the first retraining free
machine unlearning method to require only the unlabelled input samples for the forget set. By not
requiring the long-term storage of the retain dataset, a labelled forget set, or the loss over the forget
set, LFSSD is lightweight, robust and more practically useful than its predecessors.

Benchmarks. We evaluate LFSSD in the same manner as Chundawat et al. (2023a); Foster et al.
(2023), comparing against a baseline model without any unlearning, a model retrained from scratch
on only Dr, a model finetuned for 2 epochs on Dr, and several existing state-of-the-art methods
(Chundawat et al., 2023a; Graves et al., 2021; Foster et al., 2023) (teacher, amnesiac, SSD). Three
key tasks are evaluated using ResNet18 (RN) and Vision Transformer (ViT): full class, subclass,
and random forgetting. Fullclass entails forgetting an entire class from the dataset (e.g. rocket from
Cifar100), subclass involves forgetting a related subclass from the dataset (e.g. all rockets from class
Vehicle2 in Cifar20), and random forgetting selects a random subset of samples across all classes.
Datasets used include the Cifar suite (Krizhevsky & Hinton, 2010), and the PINS face recognition
dataset (Burak, 2020). Runs are repeated 10 times for each method, with the mean and standard
deviation shown in the tables. Dr and Df in the tables denote the accuracy on the respective subset
of data in percent. Since SSD (and therefore LFSSD) is deterministic, there is no standard deviation

across repeated runs. We use the same membership inference attack as in Chundawat et al. (2023a);
Foster et al. (2023), where logistic regression is used to classify samples as seen or unseen for a
given model, based the entropy of the model outputs for that sample.

Resources. A single backward pass over the full dataset D is O(bf ull· p) where bf ullis the number
of batches in the dataset and p is the number of parameters in the model. Similarly, the complexity
for the forget and retain set is O(bf orget· p) and O(bretain · p), respectively. Note that bretain ≈
bf ull>> bf orget. SSD requires only one computation of the gradients for D (can be saved and
reused), then for every forget request it requires one computation forDf to then apply the dampening
in O(bf orget· p).

LFSSD has the same complexity as SSD with the difference being that LFSSD calculates the norm
of the output instead of the loss. In practice, this is similar in compute time.

Other methods are retraining-based and depend on the number of epochs N, generally on the order
of O(N · bretain · p), which is much larger.

Sensitivity analysis. The values for alpha and lambda for SSD are taken from Foster et al. (2023)
where the authors used Optuna to search for ideal parameters. For LFSSD we performed a simplified
hyperparameter search keeping lambda fixed at 1 and alpha values [1, 50]. We pick one value per
unlearning task (e.g. full class, sub-class, random) to show robustness across classes and do not
use the best alpha per individual class/subclass (e.g., taking alpha 25 for rocket, alpha 5 for another
class, etc.). A sensitivity analysis in Table 2 on CIFAR100 rocket class unlearning shows that there
is a significant drop off in performance when picking an alpha that is too aggressive or conservative
but the method has a wide plateau in which it performs well.

Unlearning scenarios without labels. For cases where labels are hard to get we expect two main
scenarios: First, having a catalogue of undesired/copyrighted data (e.g., images) that we want to
unlearn from the model just to be on the safe side legally even if it might not be in the model. In this
case, we do not have the labels. Second, models that were trained with semi-supervised learning
could benefit from our method when we do not want to rely on the accuracy of pseudo labels.

excerpts.text:
ABSTRACT

We present a machine unlearning approach that is both retraining- and label-free.
Most existing machine unlearning approaches require a model to be fine-tuned
to remove information while preserving performance. This is computationally
expensive and necessitates the storage of the whole dataset for the lifetime of
the model. Retraining-free approaches often utilise Fisher information, which
is derived from the loss and requires labelled data which may not be available.
Thus, we present an extension to the Selective Synaptic Dampening algorithm,
substituting the diagonal of the Fisher information matrix for the gradient of the
l2 norm of the model output to approximate sensitivity. We evaluate our method
in a range of experiments using ResNet18 and Vision Transformer. Results show
our label-free method is competitive with existing state-of-the-art approaches.
excerpts.heading: ABSTRACT

excerpts.text:
1 I NTRODUCTION & RELATED WORK

With increasing regulations around machine learning, the ability for a trained model to forget private
or harmful information is essential. This task is typically formulated by splitting some training
dataset D into a subset of data that needs to be forgotten Df , and the retained data Dr = D \ Df .
The objective is to forget Df from the model, while simultaneously preserving model performance
on Dr (Cao & Yang, 2015). To solve this problem, several methods have been proposed that disrupt
the model’s functional mapping for samples in Df (e.g. by learning random labels), while also
training for a small number of epochs over Dr to repair or protect performance (Chundawat et al.,
2023a;b; Graves et al., 2021; Tarun et al., 2023; Kurmanji et al., 2023). This is computationally
expensive and requires the storage of the full dataset permanently. In contrast, recent methods such
as FisherForgetting from Golatkar et al. (2020) or Selective Synaptic Dampening (SSD) from Foster
et al. (2023) have explored retraining-free approaches, with the latter achieving state-of-the-art
performance. These often involve estimating the importance of parameters for the forget set,
allowing them to be disrupted through noise or dampening, but without destroying performance
on the retain set. Parameter importance estimation is typically achieved via the diagonal of the
Fisher information matrix (FIM), which in practice is calculated as the square of the first-order
gradients of the loss. This requires access to a ground truth label, which may not always be
available. Therefore, we propose a novel extension of SSD that does not require access to the loss
or ground truth labels, which we refer to as Loss-Free Selective Synaptic Dampening (LFSSD).
LFSSD replaces the Fisher-based importance estimation with an approximation of the sensitivity of
the model to perturbations of each parameter, which may be interpreted as parameter importance.
Such importance estimation has been shown to be effective in continual learning (Aljundi et al.,
2018), yet it has not been applied in unlearning. Here, we show this new approach to dampening
important parameters is equally effective as Fisher information, without relying on labelled data.
To the best of our knowledge, LFSSD is the first retraining-free unlearning method to require only
the unlabelled forget samples at forgetting time.

Which we can calculate over D and Df and substitute into equation 1 in place of [] and []f . Results
can be seen in Table 1, with further results available in the appendix. The objective is to maximise
the Dr accuracy while having a low membership inference attack score (MIA) similar to the retrain

lead to the Streisand effect (e.g., labelling a cat as a boat is an obvious modification) (Chundawat
et al., 2023a). The results show that LFSSD produces scores similar to that of a model trained
on only Dr, and is competitive with state-of-the-art methods such as SSD, while being the first
method to require no labelled data and no retraining. A shared limitation with SSD is the reliance
on choosing α and λ values that balance forgetting and model performance.

excerpts.text:
3 C ONCLUSION

Developing lightweight yet effective machine unlearning approaches is a significant open problem.
In this work, we presented a novel extension of existing literature that is the first retraining free
machine unlearning method to require only the unlabelled input samples for the forget set. By not
requiring the long-term storage of the retain dataset, a labelled forget set, or the loss over the forget
set, LFSSD is lightweight, robust and more practically useful than its predecessors.

Resources. A single backward pass over the full dataset D is O(bf ull· p) where bf ullis the number
of batches in the dataset and p is the number of parameters in the model. Similarly, the complexity
for the forget and retain set is O(bf orget· p) and O(bretain · p), respectively. Note that bretain ≈
bf ull>> bf orget. SSD requires only one computation of the gradients for D (can be saved and
reused), then for every forget request it requires one computation forDf to then apply the dampening
in O(bf orget· p).

LFSSD has the same complexity as SSD with the difference being that LFSSD calculates the norm
of the output instead of the loss. In practice, this is similar in compute time.

Other methods are retraining-based and depend on the number of epochs N, generally on the order
of O(N · bretain · p), which is much larger.

Sensitivity analysis. The values for alpha and lambda for SSD are taken from Foster et al. (2023)
where the authors used Optuna to search for ideal parameters. For LFSSD we performed a simplified
hyperparameter search keeping lambda fixed at 1 and alpha values [1, 50]. We pick one value per
unlearning task (e.g. full class, sub-class, random) to show robustness across classes and do not
use the best alpha per individual class/subclass (e.g., taking alpha 25 for rocket, alpha 5 for another
class, etc.). A sensitivity analysis in Table 2 on CIFAR100 rocket class unlearning shows that there
is a significant drop off in performance when picking an alpha that is too aggressive or conservative
but the method has a wide plateau in which it performs well.

Unlearning scenarios without labels. For cases where labels are hard to get we expect two main
scenarios: First, having a catalogue of undesired/copyrighted data (e.g., images) that we want to
unlearn from the model just to be on the safe side legally even if it might not be in the model. In this
case, we do not have the labels. Second, models that were trained with semi-supervised learning
could benefit from our method when we do not want to rely on the accuracy of pseudo labels.

LOSS -FREE MACHINE UNLEARNING

Jack Foster∗1,2, Stefan Schoepf ∗1,2 & Alexandra Brintrup 1,2

excerpts.text:
ABSTRACT

We present a machine unlearning approach that is both retraining- and label-free.
Most existing machine unlearning approaches require a model to be fine-tuned
to remove information while preserving performance. This is computationally
expensive and necessitates the storage of the whole dataset for the lifetime of
the model. Retraining-free approaches often utilise Fisher information, which
is derived from the loss and requires labelled data which may not be available.
Thus, we present an extension to the Selective Synaptic Dampening algorithm,
substituting the diagonal of the Fisher information matrix for the gradient of the
l2 norm of the model output to approximate sensitivity. We evaluate our method
in a range of experiments using ResNet18 and Vision Transformer. Results show
our label-free method is competitive with existing state-of-the-art approaches.
excerpts.heading: ABSTRACT

excerpts.text:
1 I NTRODUCTION & RELATED WORK

With increasing regulations around machine learning, the ability for a trained model to forget private
or harmful information is essential. This task is typically formulated by splitting some training
dataset D into a subset of data that needs to be forgotten Df , and the retained data Dr = D \ Df .
The objective is to forget Df from the model, while simultaneously preserving model performance
on Dr (Cao & Yang, 2015). To solve this problem, several methods have been proposed that disrupt
the model’s functional mapping for samples in Df (e.g. by learning random labels), while also
training for a small number of epochs over Dr to repair or protect performance (Chundawat et al.,
2023a;b; Graves et al., 2021; Tarun et al., 2023; Kurmanji et al., 2023). This is computationally
expensive and requires the storage of the full dataset permanently. In contrast, recent methods such
as FisherForgetting from Golatkar et al. (2020) or Selective Synaptic Dampening (SSD) from Foster
et al. (2023) have explored retraining-free approaches, with the latter achieving state-of-the-art
performance. These often involve estimating the importance of parameters for the forget set,
allowing them to be disrupted through noise or dampening, but without destroying performance
on the retain set. Parameter importance estimation is typically achieved via the diagonal of the
Fisher information matrix (FIM), which in practice is calculated as the square of the first-order
gradients of the loss. This requires access to a ground truth label, which may not always be
available. Therefore, we propose a novel extension of SSD that does not require access to the loss
or ground truth labels, which we refer to as Loss-Free Selective Synaptic Dampening (LFSSD).
LFSSD replaces the Fisher-based importance estimation with an approximation of the sensitivity of
the model to perturbations of each parameter, which may be interpreted as parameter importance.
Such importance estimation has been shown to be effective in continual learning (Aljundi et al.,
2018), yet it has not been applied in unlearning. Here, we show this new approach to dampening
important parameters is equally effective as Fisher information, without relying on labelled data.
To the best of our knowledge, LFSSD is the first retraining-free unlearning method to require only
the unlabelled forget samples at forgetting time.

Which we can calculate over D and Df and substitute into equation 1 in place of [] and []f . Results
can be seen in Table 1, with further results available in the appendix. The objective is to maximise
the Dr accuracy while having a low membership inference attack score (MIA) similar to the retrain

lead to the Streisand effect (e.g., labelling a cat as a boat is an obvious modification) (Chundawat
et al., 2023a). The results show that LFSSD produces scores similar to that of a model trained
on only Dr, and is competitive with state-of-the-art methods such as SSD, while being the first
method to require no labelled data and no retraining. A shared limitation with SSD is the reliance
on choosing α and λ values that balance forgetting and model performance.

excerpts.text:
3 C ONCLUSION

Developing lightweight yet effective machine unlearning approaches is a significant open problem.
In this work, we presented a novel extension of existing literature that is the first retraining free
machine unlearning method to require only the unlabelled input samples for the forget set. By not
requiring the long-term storage of the retain dataset, a labelled forget set, or the loss over the forget
set, LFSSD is lightweight, robust and more practically useful than its predecessors.

Benchmarks. We evaluate LFSSD in the same manner as Chundawat et al. (2023a); Foster et al.
(2023), comparing against a baseline model without any unlearning, a model retrained from scratch

(Chundawat et al., 2023a; Graves et al., 2021; Foster et al., 2023) (teacher, amnesiac, SSD). Three
key tasks are evaluated using ResNet18 (RN) and Vision Transformer (ViT): full class, subclass,
and random forgetting. Fullclass entails forgetting an entire class from the dataset (e.g. rocket from

Resources. A single backward pass over the full dataset D is O(bf ull· p) where bf ullis the number
of batches in the dataset and p is the number of parameters in the model. Similarly, the complexity
for the forget and retain set is O(bf orget· p) and O(bretain · p), respectively. Note that bretain ≈
bf ull>> bf orget. SSD requires only one computation of the gradients for D (can be saved and
reused), then for every forget request it requires one computation forDf to then apply the dampening
in O(bf orget· p).

LFSSD has the same complexity as SSD with the difference being that LFSSD calculates the norm
of the output instead of the loss. In practice, this is similar in compute time.

Other methods are retraining-based and depend on the number of epochs N, generally on the order
of O(N · bretain · p), which is much larger.

Sensitivity analysis. The values for alpha and lambda for SSD are taken from Foster et al. (2023)
where the authors used Optuna to search for ideal parameters. For LFSSD we performed a simplified
hyperparameter search keeping lambda fixed at 1 and alpha values [1, 50]. We pick one value per
unlearning task (e.g. full class, sub-class, random) to show robustness across classes and do not
use the best alpha per individual class/subclass (e.g., taking alpha 25 for rocket, alpha 5 for another
class, etc.). A sensitivity analysis in Table 2 on CIFAR100 rocket class unlearning shows that there
is a significant drop off in performance when picking an alpha that is too aggressive or conservative
but the method has a wide plateau in which it performs well.

Unlearning scenarios without labels. For cases where labels are hard to get we expect two main
scenarios: First, having a catalogue of undesired/copyrighted data (e.g., images) that we want to
unlearn from the model just to be on the safe side legally even if it might not be in the model. In this
case, we do not have the labels. Second, models that were trained with semi-supervised learning
could benefit from our method when we do not want to rely on the accuracy of pseudo labels.

LOSS -FREE MACHINE UNLEARNING

Jack Foster∗1,2, Stefan Schoepf ∗1,2 & Alexandra Brintrup 1,2
1Department of Engineering, University of Cambridge
2The Alan Turing Institute
*Indicates equal contribution
{jwf40,ss2823,ab702}@cam.ac.uk
excerpts.heading: Accepted as a Tiny Paper at ICLR 2024 (Preprint)

excerpts.text:
ABSTRACT

We present a machine unlearning approach that is both retraining- and label-free.
Most existing machine unlearning approaches require a model to be fine-tuned
to remove information while preserving performance. This is computationally
expensive and necessitates the storage of the whole dataset for the lifetime of
the model. Retraining-free approaches often utilise Fisher information, which
is derived from the loss and requires labelled data which may not be available.
Thus, we present an extension to the Selective Synaptic Dampening algorithm,
substituting the diagonal of the Fisher information matrix for the gradient of the
l2 norm of the model output to approximate sensitivity. We evaluate our method
in a range of experiments using ResNet18 and Vision Transformer. Results show
our label-free method is competitive with existing state-of-the-art approaches.
excerpts.heading: ABSTRACT

excerpts.text:
1 I NTRODUCTION & RELATED WORK

With increasing regulations around machine learning, the ability for a trained model to forget private
or harmful information is essential. This task is typically formulated by splitting some training
dataset D into a subset of data that needs to be forgotten Df , and the retained data Dr = D \ Df .
The objective is to forget Df from the model, while simultaneously preserving model performance
on Dr (Cao & Yang, 2015). To solve this problem, several methods have been proposed that disrupt
the model’s functional mapping for samples in Df (e.g. by learning random labels), while also
training for a small number of epochs over Dr to repair or protect performance (Chundawat et al.,
2023a;b; Graves et al., 2021; Tarun et al., 2023; Kurmanji et al., 2023). This is computationally
expensive and requires the storage of the full dataset permanently. In contrast, recent methods such
as FisherForgetting from Golatkar et al. (2020) or Selective Synaptic Dampening (SSD) from Foster
et al. (2023) have explored retraining-free approaches, with the latter achieving state-of-the-art
performance. These often involve estimating the importance of parameters for the forget set,
allowing them to be disrupted through noise or dampening, but without destroying performance
on the retain set. Parameter importance estimation is typically achieved via the diagonal of the
Fisher information matrix (FIM), which in practice is calculated as the square of the first-order
gradients of the loss. This requires access to a ground truth label, which may not always be
available. Therefore, we propose a novel extension of SSD that does not require access to the loss
or ground truth labels, which we refer to as Loss-Free Selective Synaptic Dampening (LFSSD).
LFSSD replaces the Fisher-based importance estimation with an approximation of the sensitivity of
the model to perturbations of each parameter, which may be interpreted as parameter importance.
Such importance estimation has been shown to be effective in continual learning (Aljundi et al.,
2018), yet it has not been applied in unlearning. Here, we show this new approach to dampening
important parameters is equally effective as Fisher information, without relying on labelled data.
To the best of our knowledge, LFSSD is the first retraining-free unlearning method to require only
the unlabelled forget samples at forgetting time.

over both D and Df , we can select parameters that are disproportionately important for the forget

Which we can calculate over D and Df and substitute into equation 1 in place of [] and []f . Results
can be seen in Table 1, with further results available in the appendix. The objective is to maximise
the Dr accuracy while having a low membership inference attack score (MIA) similar to the retrain
column (Shokri et al., 2017). Similarity to the retrained model is necessary, as ”over-forgetting” can
lead to the Streisand effect (e.g., labelling a cat as a boat is an obvious modification) (Chundawat
et al., 2023a). The results show that LFSSD produces scores similar to that of a model trained
on only Dr, and is competitive with state-of-the-art methods such as SSD, while being the first
method to require no labelled data and no retraining. A shared limitation with SSD is the reliance
on choosing α and λ values that balance forgetting and model performance.

excerpts.text:
3 C ONCLUSION

Developing lightweight yet effective machine unlearning approaches is a significant open problem.
In this work, we presented a novel extension of existing literature that is the first retraining free
machine unlearning method to require only the unlabelled input samples for the forget set. By not
requiring the long-term storage of the retain dataset, a labelled forget set, or the loss over the forget
set, LFSSD is lightweight, robust and more practically useful than its predecessors.

Benchmarks. We evaluate LFSSD in the same manner as Chundawat et al. (2023a); Foster et al.
(2023), comparing against a baseline model without any unlearning, a model retrained from scratch
on only Dr, a model finetuned for 2 epochs on Dr, and several existing state-of-the-art methods
(Chundawat et al., 2023a; Graves et al., 2021; Foster et al., 2023) (teacher, amnesiac, SSD). Three
key tasks are evaluated using ResNet18 (RN) and Vision Transformer (ViT): full class, subclass,
and random forgetting. Fullclass entails forgetting an entire class from the dataset (e.g. rocket from
Cifar100), subclass involves forgetting a related subclass from the dataset (e.g. all rockets from class
Vehicle2 in Cifar20), and random forgetting selects a random subset of samples across all classes.
Datasets used include the Cifar suite (Krizhevsky & Hinton, 2010), and the PINS face recognition
dataset (Burak, 2020). Runs are repeated 10 times for each method, with the mean and standard
deviation shown in the tables. Dr and Df in the tables denote the accuracy on the respective subset
of data in percent. Since SSD (and therefore LFSSD) is deterministic, there is no standard deviation

across repeated runs. We use the same membership inference attack as in Chundawat et al. (2023a);

Resources. A single backward pass over the full dataset D is O(bf ull· p) where bf ullis the number
of batches in the dataset and p is the number of parameters in the model. Similarly, the complexity
for the forget and retain set is O(bf orget· p) and O(bretain · p), respectively. Note that bretain ≈
bf ull>> bf orget. SSD requires only one computation of the gradients for D (can be saved and
reused), then for every forget request it requires one computation forDf to then apply the dampening
in O(bf orget· p).

LFSSD has the same complexity as SSD with the difference being that LFSSD calculates the norm
of the output instead of the loss. In practice, this is similar in compute time.

Other methods are retraining-based and depend on the number of epochs N, generally on the order
of O(N · bretain · p), which is much larger.

Sensitivity analysis. The values for alpha and lambda for SSD are taken from Foster et al. (2023)
where the authors used Optuna to search for ideal parameters. For LFSSD we performed a simplified
hyperparameter search keeping lambda fixed at 1 and alpha values [1, 50]. We pick one value per
unlearning task (e.g. full class, sub-class, random) to show robustness across classes and do not
use the best alpha per individual class/subclass (e.g., taking alpha 25 for rocket, alpha 5 for another
class, etc.). A sensitivity analysis in Table 2 on CIFAR100 rocket class unlearning shows that there
is a significant drop off in performance when picking an alpha that is too aggressive or conservative
but the method has a wide plateau in which it performs well.

Unlearning scenarios without labels. For cases where labels are hard to get we expect two main
scenarios: First, having a catalogue of undesired/copyrighted data (e.g., images) that we want to
unlearn from the model just to be on the safe side legally even if it might not be in the model. In this
case, we do not have the labels. Second, models that were trained with semi-supervised learning
could benefit from our method when we do not want to rely on the accuracy of pseudo labels.

LOSS -FREE MACHINE UNLEARNING

Jack Foster∗1,2, Stefan Schoepf ∗1,2 & Alexandra Brintrup 1,2

excerpts.heading: Accepted as a Tiny Paper at ICLR 2024 (Preprint)

excerpts.text:
ABSTRACT

We present a machine unlearning approach that is both retraining- and label-free.
Most existing machine unlearning approaches require a model to be fine-tuned
to remove information while preserving performance. This is computationally
expensive and necessitates the storage of the whole dataset for the lifetime of
the model. Retraining-free approaches often utilise Fisher information, which
is derived from the loss and requires labelled data which may not be available.
Thus, we present an extension to the Selective Synaptic Dampening algorithm,
substituting the diagonal of the Fisher information matrix for the gradient of the
l2 norm of the model output to approximate sensitivity. We evaluate our method
in a range of experiments using ResNet18 and Vision Transformer. Results show
our label-free method is competitive with existing state-of-the-art approaches.
excerpts.heading: ABSTRACT

excerpts.text:
1 I NTRODUCTION & RELATED WORK

With increasing regulations around machine learning, the ability for a trained model to forget private
or harmful information is essential. This task is typically formulated by splitting some training
dataset D into a subset of data that needs to be forgotten Df , and the retained data Dr = D \ Df .
The objective is to forget Df from the model, while simultaneously preserving model performance
on Dr (Cao & Yang, 2015). To solve this problem, several methods have been proposed that disrupt
the model’s functional mapping for samples in Df (e.g. by learning random labels), while also
training for a small number of epochs over Dr to repair or protect performance (Chundawat et al.,
2023a;b; Graves et al., 2021; Tarun et al., 2023; Kurmanji et al., 2023). This is computationally
expensive and requires the storage of the full dataset permanently. In contrast, recent methods such
as FisherForgetting from Golatkar et al. (2020) or Selective Synaptic Dampening (SSD) from Foster
et al. (2023) have explored retraining-free approaches, with the latter achieving state-of-the-art
performance. These often involve estimating the importance of parameters for the forget set,
allowing them to be disrupted through noise or dampening, but without destroying performance
on the retain set. Parameter importance estimation is typically achieved via the diagonal of the
Fisher information matrix (FIM), which in practice is calculated as the square of the first-order
gradients of the loss. This requires access to a ground truth label, which may not always be
available. Therefore, we propose a novel extension of SSD that does not require access to the loss
or ground truth labels, which we refer to as Loss-Free Selective Synaptic Dampening (LFSSD).
LFSSD replaces the Fisher-based importance estimation with an approximation of the sensitivity of
the model to perturbations of each parameter, which may be interpreted as parameter importance.
Such importance estimation has been shown to be effective in continual learning (Aljundi et al.,
2018), yet it has not been applied in unlearning. Here, we show this new approach to dampening
important parameters is equally effective as Fisher information, without relying on labelled data.
To the best of our knowledge, LFSSD is the first retraining-free unlearning method to require only
the unlabelled forget samples at forgetting time.

over both D and Df , we can select parameters that are disproportionately important for the forget

Which we can calculate over D and Df and substitute into equation 1 in place of [] and []f . Results
can be seen in Table 1, with further results available in the appendix. The objective is to maximise
the Dr accuracy while having a low membership inference attack score (MIA) similar to the retrain
column (Shokri et al., 2017). Similarity to the retrained model is necessary, as ”over-forgetting” can
lead to the Streisand effect (e.g., labelling a cat as a boat is an obvious modification) (Chundawat
et al., 2023a). The results show that LFSSD produces scores similar to that of a model trained
on only Dr, and is competitive with state-of-the-art methods such as SSD, while being the first
method to require no labelled data and no retraining. A shared limitation with SSD is the reliance
on choosing α and λ values that balance forgetting and model performance.

excerpts.text:
3 C ONCLUSION

Developing lightweight yet effective machine unlearning approaches is a significant open problem.
In this work, we presented a novel extension of existing literature that is the first retraining free
machine unlearning method to require only the unlabelled input samples for the forget set. By not
requiring the long-term storage of the retain dataset, a labelled forget set, or the loss over the forget
set, LFSSD is lightweight, robust and more practically useful than its predecessors.

(2023), comparing against a baseline model without any unlearning, a model retrained from scratch

(Chundawat et al., 2023a; Graves et al., 2021; Foster et al., 2023) (teacher, amnesiac, SSD). Three
key tasks are evaluated using ResNet18 (RN) and Vision Transformer (ViT): full class, subclass,
and random forgetting. Fullclass entails forgetting an entire class from the dataset (e.g. rocket from

Resources. A single backward pass over the full dataset D is O(bf ull· p) where bf ullis the number
of batches in the dataset and p is the number of parameters in the model. Similarly, the complexity
for the forget and retain set is O(bf orget· p) and O(bretain · p), respectively. Note that bretain ≈
bf ull>> bf orget. SSD requires only one computation of the gradients for D (can be saved and
reused), then for every forget request it requires one computation forDf to then apply the dampening
in O(bf orget· p).

LFSSD has the same complexity as SSD with the difference being that LFSSD calculates the norm
of the output instead of the loss. In practice, this is similar in compute time.

Other methods are retraining-based and depend on the number of epochs N, generally on the order
of O(N · bretain · p), which is much larger.

Sensitivity analysis. The values for alpha and lambda for SSD are taken from Foster et al. (2023)
where the authors used Optuna to search for ideal parameters. For LFSSD we performed a simplified
hyperparameter search keeping lambda fixed at 1 and alpha values [1, 50]. We pick one value per
unlearning task (e.g. full class, sub-class, random) to show robustness across classes and do not
use the best alpha per individual class/subclass (e.g., taking alpha 25 for rocket, alpha 5 for another
class, etc.). A sensitivity analysis in Table 2 on CIFAR100 rocket class unlearning shows that there
is a significant drop off in performance when picking an alpha that is too aggressive or conservative
but the method has a wide plateau in which it performs well.

Unlearning scenarios without labels. For cases where labels are hard to get we expect two main
scenarios: First, having a catalogue of undesired/copyrighted data (e.g., images) that we want to
unlearn from the model just to be on the safe side legally even if it might not be in the model. In this
case, we do not have the labels. Second, models that were trained with semi-supervised learning
could benefit from our method when we do not want to rely on the accuracy of pseudo labels.

excerpts.text:
ABSTRACT

We present a machine unlearning approach that is both retraining- and label-free.
Most existing machine unlearning approaches require a model to be fine-tuned
to remove information while preserving performance. This is computationally
expensive and necessitates the storage of the whole dataset for the lifetime of
the model. Retraining-free approaches often utilise Fisher information, which
is derived from the loss and requires labelled data which may not be available.
Thus, we present an extension to the Selective Synaptic Dampening algorithm,
substituting the diagonal of the Fisher information matrix for the gradient of the
l2 norm of the model output to approximate sensitivity. We evaluate our method
in a range of experiments using ResNet18 and Vision Transformer. Results show
our label-free method is competitive with existing state-of-the-art approaches.
excerpts.heading: ABSTRACT

excerpts.text:
1 I NTRODUCTION & RELATED WORK

With increasing regulations around machine learning, the ability for a trained model to forget private
or harmful information is essential. This task is typically formulated by splitting some training
dataset D into a subset of data that needs to be forgotten Df , and the retained data Dr = D \ Df .
The objective is to forget Df from the model, while simultaneously preserving model performance
on Dr (Cao & Yang, 2015). To solve this problem, several methods have been proposed that disrupt
the model’s functional mapping for samples in Df (e.g. by learning random labels), while also
training for a small number of epochs over Dr to repair or protect performance (Chundawat et al.,
2023a;b; Graves et al., 2021; Tarun et al., 2023; Kurmanji et al., 2023). This is computationally
expensive and requires the storage of the full dataset permanently. In contrast, recent methods such
as FisherForgetting from Golatkar et al. (2020) or Selective Synaptic Dampening (SSD) from Foster
et al. (2023) have explored retraining-free approaches, with the latter achieving state-of-the-art
performance. These often involve estimating the importance of parameters for the forget set,
allowing them to be disrupted through noise or dampening, but without destroying performance
on the retain set. Parameter importance estimation is typically achieved via the diagonal of the
Fisher information matrix (FIM), which in practice is calculated as the square of the first-order
gradients of the loss. This requires access to a ground truth label, which may not always be
available. Therefore, we propose a novel extension of SSD that does not require access to the loss
or ground truth labels, which we refer to as Loss-Free Selective Synaptic Dampening (LFSSD).
LFSSD replaces the Fisher-based importance estimation with an approximation of the sensitivity of
the model to perturbations of each parameter, which may be interpreted as parameter importance.
Such importance estimation has been shown to be effective in continual learning (Aljundi et al.,
2018), yet it has not been applied in unlearning. Here, we show this new approach to dampening
important parameters is equally effective as Fisher information, without relying on labelled data.
To the best of our knowledge, LFSSD is the first retraining-free unlearning method to require only
the unlabelled forget samples at forgetting time.

Which we can calculate over D and Df and substitute into equation 1 in place of [] and []f . Results
can be seen in Table 1, with further results available in the appendix. The objective is to maximise
the Dr accuracy while having a low membership inference attack score (MIA) similar to the retrain

lead to the Streisand effect (e.g., labelling a cat as a boat is an obvious modification) (Chundawat
et al., 2023a). The results show that LFSSD produces scores similar to that of a model trained
on only Dr, and is competitive with state-of-the-art methods such as SSD, while being the first
method to require no labelled data and no retraining. A shared limitation with SSD is the reliance
on choosing α and λ values that balance forgetting and model performance.
excerpts.heading: 2 M ETHODS & R ESULTS

excerpts.text:
3 C ONCLUSION

Developing lightweight yet effective machine unlearning approaches is a significant open problem.
In this work, we presented a novel extension of existing literature that is the first retraining free
machine unlearning method to require only the unlabelled input samples for the forget set. By not
requiring the long-term storage of the retain dataset, a labelled forget set, or the loss over the forget
set, LFSSD is lightweight, robust and more practically useful than its predecessors.

Benchmarks. We evaluate LFSSD in the same manner as Chundawat et al. (2023a); Foster et al.
(2023), comparing against a baseline model without any unlearning, a model retrained from scratch
on only Dr, a model finetuned for 2 epochs on Dr, and several existing state-of-the-art methods
(Chundawat et al., 2023a; Graves et al., 2021; Foster et al., 2023) (teacher, amnesiac, SSD). Three
key tasks are evaluated using ResNet18 (RN) and Vision Transformer (ViT): full class, subclass,
and random forgetting. Fullclass entails forgetting an entire class from the dataset (e.g. rocket from
Cifar100), subclass involves forgetting a related subclass from the dataset (e.g. all rockets from class
Vehicle2 in Cifar20), and random forgetting selects a random subset of samples across all classes.
Datasets used include the Cifar suite (Krizhevsky & Hinton, 2010), and the PINS face recognition
dataset (Burak, 2020). Runs are repeated 10 times for each method, with the mean and standard
deviation shown in the tables. Dr and Df in the tables denote the accuracy on the respective subset

Resources. A single backward pass over the full dataset D is O(bf ull· p) where bf ullis the number
of batches in the dataset and p is the number of parameters in the model. Similarly, the complexity
for the forget and retain set is O(bf orget· p) and O(bretain · p), respectively. Note that bretain ≈
bf ull>> bf orget. SSD requires only one computation of the gradients for D (can be saved and
reused), then for every forget request it requires one computation forDf to then apply the dampening
in O(bf orget· p).

LFSSD has the same complexity as SSD with the difference being that LFSSD calculates the norm
of the output instead of the loss. In practice, this is similar in compute time.

Other methods are retraining-based and depend on the number of epochs N, generally on the order
of O(N · bretain · p), which is much larger.

Sensitivity analysis. The values for alpha and lambda for SSD are taken from Foster et al. (2023)
where the authors used Optuna to search for ideal parameters. For LFSSD we performed a simplified
hyperparameter search keeping lambda fixed at 1 and alpha values [1, 50]. We pick one value per
unlearning task (e.g. full class, sub-class, random) to show robustness across classes and do not
use the best alpha per individual class/subclass (e.g., taking alpha 25 for rocket, alpha 5 for another
class, etc.). A sensitivity analysis in Table 2 on CIFAR100 rocket class unlearning shows that there
is a significant drop off in performance when picking an alpha that is too aggressive or conservative
but the method has a wide plateau in which it performs well.

Unlearning scenarios without labels. For cases where labels are hard to get we expect two main
scenarios: First, having a catalogue of undesired/copyrighted data (e.g., images) that we want to
unlearn from the model just to be on the safe side legally even if it might not be in the model. In this
case, we do not have the labels. Second, models that were trained with semi-supervised learning
could benefit from our method when we do not want to rely on the accuracy of pseudo labels.

form_guidance: Open with a neutral contribution summary that authors should recognize.
Present the strongest reasons to publish before decision-critical concerns.
Assess originality and likely impact explicitly.

expectations: identify the paper's method before applying method-specific criteria

synthesis.contribution_summary: The paper proposes LFSSD, a variant of Selective Synaptic Dampening (SSD) for machine unlearning. It replaces SSD's Fisher-information importance estimate with the gradient of the squared l2 norm of the model output, a sensitivity measure from Aljundi et al. (2018). As a result, the method needs neither retraining nor labels for the forget samples. The selection and dampening rule of SSD is otherwise unchanged. The method is evaluated on ResNet18 and ViT across class, subclass, random-sample and face unlearning, with SSD, retraining and other baselines as comparisons.
synthesis.originality: The originality is incremental but honestly framed. The sensitivity measure is attributed to Aljundi et al. (2018), and the dampening procedure to the authors' prior SSD work. The new element is applying this measure to unlearning and the label-free use case this allows. The paper's statement that the measure has not been applied to unlearning is the authors' own claim. It was not verified against the literature for this review. The claim to be the 'first retraining-free method requiring only unlabelled forget samples' is hedged in the introduction ('To the best of our knowledge') but stated without the hedge in the conclusion. The related-work discussion is too brief to delimit this claim. In particular, it does not explain how LFSSD's label requirements differ from those of cited zero-shot unlearning work (Chundawat et al. 2023b). The primacy claim should be treated as unestablished until this comparison is made.
synthesis.likely_impact: Practitioners who must handle deletion requests where forget samples arrive without labels could benefit from this method. It keeps SSD's low cost and avoids retraining. Because the change is a simple substitution inside an existing algorithm, it is easy to adopt and to combine with other work on importance-based unlearning. Several factors may limit its influence. Performance depends strongly on α, which changes by task (3.5, 5 and 10). Selecting α appears to require evaluating labelled forget and retain accuracy, which is in tension with the label-free framing. The importance over the full training set D is precomputed, so the claim that the training set can be discarded depends on that one-time step. The privacy evidence rests on a single entropy-based membership inference attack.
synthesis.decision_synthesis: On the positive side, the contribution is clearly specified (Eq. 3), fits the Tiny Paper format, and is evaluated over a reasonable range of architectures and unlearning scenarios with repeated runs. In class unlearning the tables broadly support competitiveness with SSD and retraining. In some rows LFSSD forgets more completely than SSD while retain accuracy stays close to baseline; for example, on ViT lamp LFSSD reaches 0.00 forget accuracy against SSD's 36.89. On the negative side, the strongest wording ('equally effective as Fisher information', 'robust') goes beyond the evidence. The ViT subclass results are mixed. For 'baby', LFSSD's forget accuracy is close to retraining (86.81 vs 93.23), but its MIA is 1.60 against 77.37 for retraining and 77.20 for SSD, so its similarity to retraining is inconsistent across metrics. Results are reported per class without an aggregate distance-to-retrain measure. Hyperparameter handling is the most decision-relevant concern. LFSSD's α was searched per task with λ fixed at 1, while SSD's values came from prior work. The sensitivity sweep covers only CIFAR100 rocket: α=1 collapses retain accuracy to 16.87% and α=50 fails to forget. The paper does not describe a label-free way to choose α. Score-changing questions for the authors: (1) How would α be selected in deployment without labels, and was it tuned on evaluation outcomes? (2) Does computing importance over D require labels or retained data access beyond a one-time precomputation? (3) Can the privacy claims be supported with a stronger attack, such as LiRA? (4) How does LFSSD relate to prior label-free or zero-shot unlearning work, and is the primacy claim justified? Non-blocking improvements: soften 'equally effective' and discuss the ViT subclass cases; report an aggregate metric; extend the α/λ sensitivity analysis to other classes and to ViT; compare the importance rankings produced by the two measures; and document how the per-table α values were chosen.

assessments.attribution: advisory specialist findings from this review run

claim_support.reasoning: In the ViT subclass rows of Table 6, LFSSD's forget-set accuracy diverges from both SSD and the retrained model. On one row it is 31.42 versus SSD's 6.68. On another, its MIA score is 1.60 versus 77.37 for the retrained model. These gaps contradict a blanket equivalence claim. In addition, hyperparameter alpha was chosen per task, with SSD and LFSSD using different values. No timing table appears in the paper. The complexity argument alone supports the claim at the level of asymptotic cost. The compute-time claim is not quantified in the inspected text. In addition, SSD's hyperparameters were tuned with Optuna while LFSSD's were tuned with a simplified search, so the comparison is not controlled.
points: Across most tables, LFSSD's results track SSD and the retrained model. However, the claim that it is 'equally effective' is broader than the subclass results support.
The claim of similar compute time to SSD is asserted, but no timing measurements are reported.
Both the 'equally effective as Fisher' claim and the 'similar compute time' claim rest on informal assertion. No timing data or controlled head-to-head ablation is reported.

significance.reasoning: No grounded, candidate-targeted finding for this axis.

originality.reasoning: The authors credit both components to prior work. They claim novelty only for the transfer into unlearning, which is a modest but clearly positioned increment. Whether the estimator has truly never been used in unlearning is author-reported and was not verified here. The authors themselves position the work as a combination of two cited components (SSD and the Aljundi et al. estimator). The novelty is therefore the transfer and its label-free consequence. Neither the prior work nor the claim that the estimator has not been applied in unlearning was independently verified.
points: The method combines two existing components: SSD's dampening rule and the Memory Aware Synapses sensitivity estimator. The paper states this provenance openly. The novelty lies in this combination and in applying it to unlearning.

The authors frame the originality as a transfer: the importance estimator comes from continual learning, and the claimed novelty is applying it to unlearning. They do not claim to have invented the estimator.

assessments.attribution: advisory specialist findings from this review run

claim_support.reasoning: No grounded, candidate-targeted finding for this axis.

significance.reasoning: Unlearning without labels and without retraining widens the range of deployment settings. This makes the work likely useful to practitioners and to researchers building on SSD. However, the impact claims ('more practically useful') rest on argument rather than experiments in these settings. The authors name concrete settings where labels are unavailable, such as a catalogue of copyrighted data or semi-supervised models. In those settings, Fisher-based SSD cannot run.
points: Removing the label requirement has plausible practical utility. The paper names copyright catalogues and semi-supervised models as use cases, but neither scenario is evaluated.
Removing the label requirement extends SSD-style unlearning to practical scenarios that the authors motivate.

originality.reasoning: The method still requires full-dataset importance values, computed once over D. Its 'only' claim therefore holds at forgetting time, not overall. The paper also cites zero-shot unlearning work (Chundawat 2023b) without stating how LFSSD differs from it on data requirements.
points: The primacy claim of being 'first retraining-free method requiring only unlabelled forget samples' is hedged with 'to the best of our knowledge'. However, the related-work discussion in this paper is brief, and the claim needs sharper scoping.

assessments.attribution: advisory specialist findings from this review run

claim_support.reasoning: In the Table 6 'sea' rows, retrain keeps Df accuracy at about 91-95%, while LFSSD drops it to about 18-21%. The authors themselves flag this kind of over-forgetting as harmful, via the Streisand effect.
points: LFSSD's results are broadly close to SSD and retrain, but it is not uniformly 'similar to retrain'. In several Cifar20 subclass cases, forget accuracy diverges markedly from retrain.

significance.reasoning: No grounded, candidate-targeted finding for this axis.

originality.reasoning: Reusing established protocols makes the results comparable with prior work, but the evaluation design is not an original contribution.
points: The empirical-evaluation contribution follows existing benchmark protocols, so it is not novel in itself. It serves as validation of the method.

author_originality_statements.statement: ABSTRACT We present a machine unlearning approach that is both retraining- and label-free.

ABSTRACT

We present a machine unlearning approach that is both retraining- and label-free.

author_originality_statements.statement: Thus, we present an extension to the Selective Synaptic Dampening algorithm, substituting the diagonal of the Fisher information matrix for the gradient of the l2 norm of the model output to approximate sensitivity.

contribution_review.author_position:
Authors' stated position:
- [claims] “ABSTRACT We present a machine unlearning approach that is both retraining- and label-free.”
- [claims] “Thus, we present an extension to the Selective Synaptic Dampening algorithm, substituting the diagonal of the Fisher information matrix for the gradient of the l2 norm of the model output to approximate sensitivity.”
- [claims] “Therefore, we propose a novel extension of SSD that does not require access to the loss or ground truth labels, which we refer to as Loss-Free Selective Synaptic Dampening (LFSSD).”
- [claims; positioned against Aljundi et al.,
2018] “Here, we show this new approach to dampening important parameters is equally effective as Fisher information, without relying on labelled data.”
- [claims; positioned against Feb 2024, ICLR 2024, Aljundi et al.,
2018] “To the best of our knowledge, LFSSD is the first retraining-free unlearning method to require only the unlabelled forget samples at forgetting time. 1 arXiv:2402.19308v1 [cs.LG] 29 Feb 2024 Accepted as a Tiny Paper at ICLR 2024 (Preprint) Table 1: Full- (class lamp) and subclass (lamp is part of electrical devices) unlearning with α =10, λ =1 on Cifar100/20.”
